+# Copy a packaged steam.desktop, rewriting every Exec=/usr/bin/steam to a wrapper.
+#
+#   steam-desktop-override <src> <dst> <wrapper>
+#
+# Called from home.nix's steamDesktopOverride activation entry, which passes
+# /usr/share/applications/steam.desktop, ~/.local/share/applications/steam.desktop
+# and the `steam` wrapper it builds. See the wrapper's comment in home.nix for why
+# Steam needs to be launched through one at all.

+# A script here, rather than the whole file mirrored into home.nix the way
+# Zoom.desktop is: steam.desktop is ~400 lines -- Comment= in 27 languages, then
+# nine Desktop Actions each with its own set -- and the only lines that need to
+# differ are the ten Exec=. Deriving the file from the pacman one also means a
+# steam.desktop changed by a package update is picked up by the next `hms` instead

+# An unreadable source is success, not failure. That keeps "which hosts have
+# Steam" a question only system/packages.<host> answers -- the same split
+# system/thermald-setup uses for its own enable half -- so this can run
+# unconditionally on every host, including the Darwin one, and do nothing.

+

+dst=${2:?destination desktop file}
+exe=${3:?wrapper to point Exec= at}

+# activation runs on Darwin too, and while the readable-source check above means
+# sed is never reached there today, a pattern that only works under GNU sed is a

+# is how Steam opens a link in a browser. A wrapper that sanitised PATH by
+# stripping nix would trade a broken download path for broken links.

+#   ./tests/steam-env.sh /path/to/steam  # tests one you already have
+#

+# $(cat /etc/hostname): steam is a shiori-only package, and the cases are about

+# of this, so a wrapper that sets the right variables but never execs would fail
+# every case rather than passing vacuously.

+echo "PATH=$PATH"
+echo "GIO_EXTRA_MODULES=${GIO_EXTRA_MODULES-<unset>}"
+echo "GIO_MODULE_DIR=${GIO_MODULE_DIR-<unset>}"
+echo "XDG_DATA_DIRS=${XDG_DATA_DIRS-<unset>}"

+# GIO_EXTRA_MODULES set (the thing that must be dropped) and GIO_MODULE_DIR set
+# (a neighbour that must survive, so an over-broad `unset GIO_*` fails here).

+  env -i \

+    PATH="$HOME/.nix-profile/bin:/nix/var/nix/profiles/default/bin:/usr/bin:/bin" \
+    GIO_EXTRA_MODULES=/nix/store/deadbeef-gvfs/lib/gio/modules \

+bad() { n=$((n + 1)); fails=$((fails + 1)); printf '  FAILED   %s\n%s\n' "$1" "$2"; }
+skip() { skips=$((skips + 1)); printf '  skipped  %s (%s)\n' "$1" "$2"; }

+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+# Copy a packaged steam.desktop, rewriting every Exec=/usr/bin/steam to a wrapper.
+#
+#   steam-desktop-override <src> <dst> <wrapper>
+#
+# Called from home.nix's steamDesktopOverride activation entry, which passes
+# /usr/share/applications/steam.desktop, ~/.local/share/applications/steam.desktop
+# and the `steam` wrapper it builds. See the wrapper's comment in home.nix for why
+# Steam needs to be launched through one at all.

+# A script here, rather than the whole file mirrored into home.nix the way
+# Zoom.desktop is: steam.desktop is ~400 lines -- Comment= in 27 languages, then
+# nine Desktop Actions each with its own set -- and the only lines that need to
+# differ are the ten Exec=. Deriving the file from the pacman one also means a
+# steam.desktop changed by a package update is picked up by the next `hms` instead
+# of silently drifting from a copy in this repo.
+#
+# An unreadable source is success, not failure. That keeps "which hosts have
+# Steam" a question only system/packages.<host> answers -- the same split
+# system/thermald-setup uses for its own enable half -- so this can run
+# unconditionally on every host, including the Darwin one, and do nothing.
+set -eu
+
+src=${1:?source desktop file}
+dst=${2:?destination desktop file}
+exe=${3:?wrapper to point Exec= at}

+# activation runs on Darwin too, and while the readable-source check above means
+# sed is never reached there today, a pattern that only works under GNU sed is a
+# trap for whoever moves this next. Anchoring also does the job \b was for --
+# neither matches a hypothetical Exec=/usr/bin/steamfoo.

+# read is the same as no override at all.

+trap - EXIT

+echo "GIO_MODULE_DIR=${GIO_MODULE_DIR-<unset>}"

# /etc/profile

# Append "$1" to $PATH when not already in.
# This function API is accessible to scripts in /etc/profile.d
append_path () {
    case ":$PATH:" in
        *:"$1":*)
            ;;
        *)
            PATH="${PATH:+$PATH:}$1"
    esac
}

# Append our default paths
append_path '/usr/local/sbin'
append_path '/usr/local/bin'
append_path '/usr/bin'

# Force PATH to be environment
export PATH

# 
# Load profiles from /etc/profile.d
if test -d /etc/profile.d/; then
	for profile in /etc/profile.d/*.sh; do
		test -r "$profile" && . "$profile"
	done
	unset profile
fi

# unset GLOBSORT, before anything else is sourced
# This variable will be part of bash => 5.3
# The rationale is that the user should always be able 
# to expect that the snippets be processed in a deterministic order.
unset -v GLOBSORT

# Unload our profile API functions
unset -f append_path

# Source global bash config, when interactive but not posix or sh mode
if test "$BASH" &&\
   test "$PS1" &&\
   test -z "$POSIXLY_CORRECT" &&\
   test "${0#-}" != sh &&\
   test -r /etc/bash.bashrc
then
	. /etc/bash.bashrc
fi

# Termcap is outdated, old, and crusty, kill it.
unset TERMCAP

# Man is much better than us at figuring this out

## NO EMAILS

**Never write an email address into anything.** Not into files, commit messages,
docs, notes, handoffs or scratch files — mine, colleagues', or service accounts.
This repo is public, and an address is a durable identifier that spreads: it
leaks the work/personal boundary, it enumerates people, and once written it gets
copied onward.

Refer to an account by its **role** — "the personal Google account", "the work
account", "the project's GCS service agent" — or record the command that
recovers the identity at read time (`gcloud config get-value account`) rather
than pasting its output. Role-based wording is better documentation anyway: "must
be the personal account, not the work one" survives an address change; a pasted
address does not.

If an address seems genuinely load-bearing, ask first.

The exception is the git identity already configured in `home.nix`, which git
requires and which is on every commit regardless.

## Commit and Push Policy

This is a personal dotfiles repo on `master`. When asked to commit and push, do both without asking for confirmation. The global "ask before public communications" rule does not apply here.

## Applying config: use `hms`, not `home-manager switch`

`hms` (defined in `home.nix`, documented in `README.md`) pushes, waits for the
commit's CI run on `forge.ko.ag`, then switches — so the switch is a download of
the closure the in-cluster runner built, not a local compile. Expect it to block
for ten-odd minutes. `hms --local` builds here instead.

It refuses on a dirty tree and on a checkout behind `origin/master`. **Both
refusals are the feature.** CI can only build a pushed commit, so do not route
around them with a bare `home-manager switch` — commit and push, or pass
`--local` deliberately and say that you did.

If a run goes red, `hms` prints the job's `error:` lines; read those rather than
re-running blind. Background on why CI is worth waiting for — and the 600s attic
transfer ceiling that made it unreliable for its first 61 runs — is in
`docs/ci-nix-home.md`.

home: launch Steam through a wrapper that prefers the host's helpers

Steam is the pacman package, but it inherits a PATH whose first entry is
~/.nix-profile/bin, and that breaks it in one measured way. Steam shells out to
`xdg-user-dir DOWNLOAD` to find the download directory; xdg.userDirs.enable puts
nix's xdg-user-dirs in the profile, so the call resolves to the nix binary, which
Steam's runtime then forces against the host's libc. Measured on shiori
2026-09-28, once per launch:

  xdg-user-dir: symbol lookup error: /usr/lib/libc.so.6: undefined symbol:
  __pointer_chk_guard, version GLIBC_PRIVATE

nix's glibc exports that GLIBC_PRIVATE symbol and Arch's does not, so a
nix-glibc-built binary cannot run against the host's copy at all.

The fix prepends the host's own directories rather than sanitising nix out of
PATH, and the difference is load-bearing: `xdg-open` exists ONLY in the profile
here, because Arch's xdg-utils is not installed, and it is how Steam opens a link
in a browser. A wrapper that stripped nix would trade a broken download path for
broken links. Prepending is also what spares this a list of which helpers to
redirect -- every name the host also provides resolves to the host's copy, and
nix keeps everything else.

GIO_EXTRA_MODULES (env.nix) is unset for the same reason in the other direction:
nix's gvfs module is built against a newer glib than either Arch's or the sniper
runtime's, so steamwebhelper logged `libgvfscommon.so: undefined symbol:
g_task_set_static_name` twice per launch. Steam's client UI is CEF, not GTK, so
the removable-drive volume monitor that variable exists for buys Steam nothing.
It goes by name, not by a GIO_* sweep, so GIO_MODULE_DIR survives.

Env, not argv, is what the wrapper changes -- which is what makes it survive the
launch paths STEAM_FORCE_DESKTOPUI_SCALING was chosen for in 10fabaf. The tray's
"restart Steam" re-execs the client, and an exec inherits the environment while
argv is rebuilt, so the PATH fix holds across it where a -flag would not.

home/steam-desktop-override is the other half: elephant/walker and xdg-open exec
the desktop file's Exec= line, not $PATH, so the wrapper is dead weight to them
until something points at it. It rewrites the pacman file at activation instead of
mirroring it -- steam.desktop is ~400 lines, Comment= in 27 languages then nine
Desktop Actions with their own, and the only lines that need to differ are the ten
Exec=. Deriving it also means a steam.desktop changed by a package update is
picked up by the next `hms` rather than drifting from a copy kept here. Its gate is
whether the source is readable, not the hostname, so the activation entry runs
everywhere and does nothing on a host without Steam -- the same split
system/thermald-setup uses for its own enable half.

The wrapper itself is shiori-only, because that is the only host whose package
list asks for Steam; elsewhere it would be a `steam` command that only ever fails
to find /usr/bin/steam.

tests/steam-env.sh drives both halves through 26 cases, and every expectation was
checked against a mutation that should break it. Five on the wrapper: dropping the
PATH prepend restores the original symbol-lookup error (caught via readlink, since
~/.nix-profile/bin entries are symlinks and an assertion on the unresolved name
passes with the bug still in place), dropping the GIO unset, sanitising nix out of
PATH entirely, unquoting "$@", and widening the unset to GIO_MODULE_DIR. Four on
the rewrite: a global sed, no chmod, no readable-source gate, no mkdir -p. All
nine fail the case that should catch them.

Security review — `git diff 10fabaf..HEAD` (commit 3aff29e) plus the uncommitted README.md change, branch `drovr/steam-nix-env`.

Verdict up front: **no Critical findings. No Important findings.** Four nits, three of them "checked and it's genuinely fine, here's why". Every one of the six categories you asked about resolves to "not a real boundary" on this machine, and I checked rather than assumed.

## Critical: none.

## Important: none.

---

## Category-by-category

### 1. The `STEAM_BIN` seam — not a privilege/trust boundary. No finding.
`/home/sauyon/devel/dotfiles/.drovr/wt/steam-nix-env/home.nix:533`
```
exec "${STEAM_BIN:-/usr/bin/steam}" "$@"
```
Concretely, who can set it: (a) the interactive shell that types `steam`; (b) the graphical session env that `elephant`/`walker` inherits, which is populated from `~/.config/environment.d`, `systemctl --user set-environment`, and the user's own shell rc; (c) a browser handing off a `steam://` URL, inheriting that same session env. Every one of those is user-writable-only, and every one of them is a position from which the attacker can already `exec` whatever they like as the user — no setuid bit, no polkit rule, no sudo anywhere in the launch path. I confirmed activation itself is unprivileged: `hms` (home.nix:792) runs `exec home-manager switch --flake …` with no `sudo`, and the only `sudo` calls in home.nix are unrelated (unix_chkpwd restore, framework-tool).

The strongest version of the objection would be "the wrapper is a `/nix/store` path, so it's integrity-protected, and `STEAM_BIN` punches a hole in that". It doesn't: the thing that decides what the launcher execs is `~/.local/share/applications/steam.desktop`, a plain user-owned 0644 file this very change writes. An attacker who can set `STEAM_BIN` can also just rewrite that `Exec=` line, which is strictly more durable (survives reboot) than an env var. The seam grants nothing that wasn't already granted. The in-code comment at home.nix:526-528 already says exactly this and is accurate.

### 2. Prepending `/usr/local/bin` — creates no hijack path here; net *reduces* hijack surface. No finding.
Checked on this machine:
```
drwxr-xr-x 1 root root 32 Sep 26 01:24 /usr/local/bin
drwxr-xr-x 1 root root 72 Sep 26 00:50 /usr/local
-r-xr-xr-x 1 root root determinate-nixd     # its sole occupant, not setuid
```
root:root 0755 at both levels. Not group- or world-writable. `id` shows the user in `wheel`, but `wheel` is not the group owner and has no write bit, so that doesn't help either. An attacker who can drop a binary in `/usr/local/bin` is already root.

Two things worth stating precisely because the framing invites a wrong answer:
- `/usr/local/bin` was **already on PATH before this change** — `/etc/profile:16` `append_path '/usr/local/bin'`. The change only moves it *earlier*, ahead of `~/.nix-profile/bin`. So the set of directories Steam searches is unchanged; only the precedence shifts.
- The precedence shift goes in the safe direction. It puts two **root-owned** directories (`/usr/local/bin`, `/usr/bin`; `/bin` is a symlink to `usr/bin`) ahead of `~/.nix-profile/bin`, a path under the user's `$HOME`. For Steam and every game and Proton prefix it launches, root-owned dirs now win name collisions where a user-path dir used to. That's a small improvement, not a regression. (`~/.nix-profile/bin` itself resolves into the read-only `/nix/store`, so it wasn't writable either — the change is neutral-to-positive, never negative.)

The one caveat, and it's about portability rather than this host: the reasoning depends on `/usr/local/bin` being root-owned, which is not universal (some sites ship it 0775 group-`staff`/`adm`, and Homebrew-style setups make it user-owned). This wrapper is gated shiori-only (home.nix:2431), so that's hypothetical today. Flagging as nit 1 below only because the code comment justifies the prepend on *symbol-resolution* grounds and never mentions that it also reorders trust.

### 3. `$exe` interpolated unquoted into the sed replacement — nit, no injection reachable.
`home/steam-desktop-override:39-41`. Walking the actual sed semantics: the replacement text is special for exactly three things — `\`, `&`, and the delimiter `|`. There is **no path to command execution**: GNU sed's `e` flag lives in the s-command's *flags* position (after the closing delimiter), not in the replacement text, so no value of `$exe` can reach it. The realistic failure modes are all loud, not silent:
- `|` in `$exe` → `unterminated 's' command`, sed exits non-zero, `set -eu` at line 22 fires, the `EXIT` trap removes the temp file, activation fails visibly.
- `&` in `$exe` → the matched text is re-inserted, producing a garbled `Exec=`. Wrong file, not code execution.
- `\1` → invalid reference, sed errors out.

And `$exe` is not attacker-influenceable: it is `"${steam}/bin/steam"` (home.nix:1961), a `/nix/store` path whose character set is `[a-z0-9+._?=-]` and `/`. Reaching it requires write access to `home.nix`, which is write access to the whole configuration — game over already, by a much shorter route.

**Crafted source desktop file:** I checked this direction separately and it's also clean. `sed` here has no `w` flag, no `e` flag, no `r`/`W` commands, and reads `$src` as data only, so no content in `/usr/share/applications/steam.desktop` can cause execution or a write outside `$tmp`. The residual "trust" question is that a malicious source file's non-`Exec=` lines are copied verbatim into a directory that outranks `/usr/share` — but the source is root-owned, and root can already put anything in `/usr/share/applications` where it would be honoured anyway. No privilege gain; see category 5.

### 4. mktemp / chmod / mv — no TOCTOU, no symlink-following. No finding.
`home/steam-desktop-override:35-47`. The sequence is correct, and correct for the non-obvious reason:
- `mktemp "$dst.XXXXXX"` opens `O_CREAT|O_EXCL` at 0600, so there's no create race and no chance of landing on an existing attacker-planted file.
- `mv -f "$tmp" "$dst"` is a `rename(2)` in the same directory. `rename` operates on the *link*, not its target — so if `$dst` is a dangling or redirected **symlink** (the exact scenario you flagged, e.g. a leftover home-manager symlink into `/nix/store`, or a user-planted symlink to `/etc/something`), it is **replaced**, not written through. This is the property that makes the whole sequence safe, and it holds.
- The `chmod 0644` → `mv` window exposes a world-readable temp file containing a derived copy of a world-readable root-owned desktop file. Nothing confidential; not a finding.
- Anyone who could win a race in `~/.local/share/applications` is the user (dir is 0755 user-owned), i.e. already has everything.
- `mkdir -p "$(dirname "$dst")"` would follow a symlinked `applications/` directory, but both the dir and any such symlink are inside `$HOME` and user-owned, so there's no boundary to cross. Worth noting this **would** be a genuine finding if activation ever ran as root; it doesn't (confirmed above), so it isn't.

I also confirmed home-manager creates `~/.local/share/applications` as a real directory with per-file symlinks inside it (it already holds the hm-managed `Zoom.desktop` from `xdg.dataFile` at home.nix:1971) rather than symlinking the directory itself — so `mv` lands in a real dir alongside hm symlinks without disturbing them. See nit 4 for the one way that coexistence could go wrong later.

### 5. Reading root-owned `/usr/share/applications/steam.desktop`, writing a derived copy into the user's dir — no trust inversion. No finding.
Direction of trust is correct: **more**-trusted source (root, 0644, not writable by the user) → **less**-trusted destination (user-owned). The dangerous direction is the reverse, and this isn't it. The derived copy does gain higher XDG precedence than its own source, but the content it carries is root's content with ten `Exec=` lines pointed at a store path; root could have written that content into `/usr/share/applications` itself. No capability is created.

### 6. THE REPO RULE (no email addresses / durable personal identifiers) — clean.
- Regex scan `[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}` over the committed diff: **no match**.
- Same scan over the uncommitted `README.md` diff: **no match**.
- Commit message body: the only address is `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>` — explicitly permitted.
- Commit *author* is `Sauyon Lee <git@sjle.co>`, which is the configured git identity covered by CLAUDE.md's stated exception ("the git identity already configured in `home.nix`, which git requires and which is on every commit regardless"). Not a violation.
- Other durable identifiers scanned for and **not** present in the diff: no `/home/<user>` literal (tests use `$HOME`), no username `sauyon`, no keys/tokens/secrets, no MAC/serial. The hostname `shiori` appears throughout, but it's an existing pervasive convention in this repo (`system/packages.shiori`, `homeConfigurations.shiori`, prior `tests/steam-ui-scaling.sh`), so it leaks nothing new.
- `2026-09-28` appears as a measurement date; that's a dated observation, not a personal identifier.

---

## Nits (4)

**nit 1 — the PATH prepend's comment doesn't mention that it reorders trust, only symbol resolution.**
`home.nix:510-521` justifies prepending entirely on the glibc/`__pointer_chk_guard` grounds, which is right but incomplete: the line also decides that `/usr/local/bin` outranks `~/.nix-profile/bin` for Steam and every child process it spawns. That's safe here (root:root 0755, verified) and safe in the safe direction, but it's a fact a future reader porting this wrapper to a host with a permissive `/usr/local/bin` would want stated. One clause would cover it.

**nit 2 — `$exe` is neither validated nor sed-escaped, and is also emitted verbatim into a `Desktop Entry` `Exec=` field.**
`home/steam-desktop-override:39-41`. Covered above for injection (unreachable). The second half is the milder one: `Exec=` has its own quoting grammar per the Desktop Entry spec, and a `$exe` containing a space would produce an ambiguous `Exec=` line that silently launches the wrong thing rather than erroring. Nix store paths never contain spaces, so this is theoretical — but the script is a standalone three-argument CLI (documented as such in its own header, and driven directly by `tests/steam-env.sh` via `$STEAM_DESKTOP_OVERRIDE`), so it will eventually be called by hand with something less well-behaved than a store path. A `case "$exe" in *[!A-Za-z0-9/._+-]*) exit 1;; esac` guard, or `printf '%s' "$exe" | sed 's/[&\\|]/\\\\&/g'`, would close both.

**nit 3 — the written `steam.desktop` is not tracked by home-manager, so it is never cleaned up. (Not security — durability.)**
Because it's an activation entry rather than `xdg.dataFile`, removing the `steam` wrapper from `home.packages` leaves `~/.local/share/applications/steam.desktop` behind forever, with `Exec=` pointing at a `/nix/store` path that the next GC deletes. The result is a launcher entry that outranks the pacman one and silently does nothing — the worst failure shape, since the file still *looks* right. (No hijack risk: store paths are hash-addressed, so a GC'd path cannot be resurrected with different content.) The comment at home.nix:1945-1949 explains why it's an activation entry — that tradeoff is defensible — but the un-uninstallability isn't mentioned anywhere.

**nit 4 — latent collision with home-manager over the same filename in the same directory.**
`~/.local/share/applications` already holds an hm-managed symlink (`Zoom.desktop`, home.nix:1971). If anyone later adds `xdg.dataFile."applications/steam.desktop"`, hm's `linkGeneration` and this `entryAfter [ "writeBoundary" ]` `mv -f` both target the identical path, and the activation entry — running second — would clobber hm's symlink, leaving hm's next-generation cleanup operating on a file it no longer recognises. Not a problem in this diff; worth a one-line "do not also declare this via xdg.dataFile" warning in the script header, since the immediately adjacent Zoom block is precisely the pattern that invites it.

## Things I checked that turned out to be nothing (stated so you know they were checked)
- `/usr/bin/steam` is `#!/bin/sh` + `exec /usr/lib/steam/steam "$@"` — absolute path, so the profile-shadowing wrapper cannot recurse into itself.
- `/usr/local/bin`'s sole occupant `determinate-nixd` is `-r-xr-xr-x root root` — not setuid, so promoting its directory to first on PATH grants nothing.
- `set -eu` + `> "$tmp"`: a failing `sed` aborts the script, the `EXIT` trap removes the temp file, and activation fails loudly rather than leaving a truncated desktop file in place. Correct.
- `[ -r "$src" ] || exit 0` also correctly no-ops on a dangling symlink source.
- `unset GIO_EXTRA_MODULES` targets exactly the variable set at `env.nix:108` and is by-name, not a `GIO_*` sweep — no collateral unset, and no security dimension either way.
- `"$@"` is quoted in the wrapper and `steam://` argv is forwarded verbatim (tests assert this) — no word-splitting of a URL into extra arguments.

- `&` in `$exe` → the matched text is re-inserted, producing a garbled `Exec=`. Wrong file, not code execution.
- `\1` → invalid reference, sed errors out.

And `$exe` is not attacker-influenceable: it is `"${steam}/bin/steam"` (home.nix:1961), a `/nix/store` path whose character set is `[a-z0-9+._?=-]` and `/`. Reaching it requires write access to `home.nix`, which is write access to the whole configuration — game over already, by a much shorter route.

**Crafted source desktop file:** I checked this direction separately and it's also clean. `sed` here has no `w` flag, no `e` flag, no `r`/`W` commands, and reads `$src` as data only, so no content in `/usr/share/applications/steam.desktop` can cause execution or a write outside `$tmp`. The residual "trust" question is that a malicious source file's non-`Exec=` lines are copied verbatim into a directory that outranks `/usr/share` — but the source is root-owned, and root can already put anything in `/usr/share/applications` where it would be honoured anyway. No privilege gain; see category 5.

### 4. mktemp / chmod / mv — no TOCTOU, no symlink-following. No finding.
`home/steam-desktop-override:35-47`. The sequence is correct, and correct for the non-obvious reason:
- `mktemp "$dst.XXXXXX"` opens `O_CREAT|O_EXCL` at 0600, so there's no create race and no chance of landing on an existing attacker-planted file.
- `mv -f "$tmp" "$dst"` is a `rename(2)` in the same directory. `rename` operates on the *link*, not its target — so if `$dst` is a dangling or redirected **symlink** (the exact scenario you flagged, e.g. a leftover home-manager symlink into `/nix/store`, or a user-planted symlink to `/etc/something`), it is **replaced**, not written through. This is the property that makes the whole sequence safe, and it holds.
- The `chmod 0644` → `mv` window exposes a world-readable temp file containing a derived copy of a world-readable root-owned desktop file. Nothing confidential; not a finding.
- Anyone who could win a race in `~/.local/share/applications` is the user (dir is 0755 user-owned), i.e. already has everything.
- `mkdir -p "$(dirname "$dst")"` would follow a symlinked `applications/` directory, but both the dir and any such symlink are inside `$HOME` and user-owned, so there's no boundary to cross. Worth noting this **would** be a genuine finding if activation ever ran as root; it doesn't (confirmed above), so it isn't.

I also confirmed home-manager creates `~/.local/share/applications` as a real directory with per-file symlinks inside it (it already holds the hm-managed `Zoom.desktop` from `xdg.dataFile` at home.nix:1971) rather than symlinking the directory itself — so `mv` lands in a real dir alongside hm symlinks without disturbing them. See nit 4 for the one way that coexistence could go wrong later.

### 5. Reading root-owned `/usr/share/applications/steam.desktop`, writing a derived copy into the user's dir — no trust inversion. No finding.
Direction of trust is correct: **more**-trusted source (root, 0644, not writable by the user) → **less**-trusted destination (user-owned). The dangerous direction is the reverse, and this isn't it. The derived copy does gain higher XDG precedence than its own source, but the content it carries is root's content with ten `Exec=` lines pointed at a store path; root could have written that content into `/usr/share/applications` itself. No capability is created.

### 6. THE REPO RULE (no email addresses / durable personal identifiers) — clean.
- Regex scan `[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}` over the committed diff: **no match**.
- Same scan over the uncommitted `README.md` diff: **no match**.
- Commit message body: the only address is `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>` — explicitly permitted.
- Commit *author* is `Sauyon Lee <git@sjle.co>`, which is the configured git identity covered by CLAUDE.md's stated exception ("the git identity already configured in `home.nix`, which git requires and which is on every commit regardless"). Not a violation.
- Other durable identifiers scanned for and **not** present in the diff: no `/home/<user>` literal (tests use `$HOME`), no username `sauyon`, no keys/tokens/secrets, no MAC/serial. The hostname `shiori` appears throughout, but it's an existing pervasive convention in this repo (`system/packages.shiori`, `homeConfigurations.shiori`, prior `tests/steam-ui-scaling.sh`), so it leaks nothing new.
- `2026-09-28` appears as a measurement date; that's a dated observation, not a personal identifier.

---

## Nits (4)

**nit 1 — the PATH prepend's comment doesn't mention that it reorders trust, only symbol resolution.**
`home.nix:510-521` justifies prepending entirely on the glibc/`__pointer_chk_guard` grounds, which is right but incomplete: the line also decides that `/usr/local/bin` outranks `~/.nix-profile/bin` for Steam and every child process it spawns. That's safe here (root:root 0755, verified) and safe in the safe direction, but it's a fact a future reader porting this wrapper to a host with a permissive `/usr/local/bin` would want stated. One clause would cover it.

**nit 2 — `$exe` is neither validated nor sed-escaped, and is also emitted verbatim into a `Desktop Entry` `Exec=` field.**
`home/steam-desktop-override:39-41`. Covered above for injection (unreachable). The second half is the milder one: `Exec=` has its own quoting grammar per the Desktop Entry spec, and a `$exe` containing a space would produce an ambiguous `Exec=` line that silently launches the wrong thing rather than erroring. Nix store paths never contain spaces, so this is theoretical — but the script is a standalone three-argument CLI (documented as such in its own header, and driven directly by `tests/steam-env.sh` via `$STEAM_DESKTOP_OVERRIDE`), so it will eventually be called by hand with something less well-behaved than a store path. A `case "$exe" in *[!A-Za-z0-9/._+-]*) exit 1;; esac` guard, or `printf '%s' "$exe" | sed 's/[&\\|]/\\\\&/g'`, would close both.

**nit 3 — the written `steam.desktop` is not tracked by home-manager, so it is never cleaned up. (Not security — durability.)**
Because it's an activation entry rather than `xdg.dataFile`, removing the `steam` wrapper from `home.packages` leaves `~/.local/share/applications/steam.desktop` behind forever, with `Exec=` pointing at a `/nix/store` path that the next GC deletes. The result is a launcher entry that outranks the pacman one and silently does nothing — the worst failure shape, since the file still *looks* right. (No hijack risk: store paths are hash-addressed, so a GC'd path cannot be resurrected with different content.) The comment at home.nix:1945-1949 explains why it's an activation entry — that tradeoff is defensible — but the un-uninstallability isn't mentioned anywhere.

**nit 4 — latent collision with home-manager over the same filename in the same directory.**
`~/.local/share/applications` already holds an hm-managed symlink (`Zoom.desktop`, home.nix:1971). If anyone later adds `xdg.dataFile."applications/steam.desktop"`, hm's `linkGeneration` and this `entryAfter [ "writeBoundary" ]` `mv -f` both target the identical path, and the activation entry — running second — would clobber hm's symlink, leaving hm's next-generation cleanup operating on a file it no longer recognises. Not a problem in this diff; worth a one-line "do not also declare this via xdg.dataFile" warning in the script header, since the immediately adjacent Zoom block is precisely the pattern that invites it.

## Things I checked that turned out to be nothing (stated so you know they were checked)
- `/usr/bin/steam` is `#!/bin/sh` + `exec /usr/lib/steam/steam "$@"` — absolute path, so the profile-shadowing wrapper cannot recurse into itself.
- `/usr/local/bin`'s sole occupant `determinate-nixd` is `-r-xr-xr-x root root` — not setuid, so promoting its directory to first on PATH grants nothing.
- `set -eu` + `> "$tmp"`: a failing `sed` aborts the script, the `EXIT` trap removes the temp file, and activation fails loudly rather than leaving a truncated desktop file in place. Correct.
- `[ -r "$src" ] || exit 0` also correctly no-ops on a dangling symlink source.
- `unset GIO_EXTRA_MODULES` targets exactly the variable set at `env.nix:108` and is by-name, not a `GIO_*` sweep — no collateral unset, and no security dimension either way.
- `"$@"` is quoted in the wrapper and `steam://` argv is forwarded verbatim (tests assert this) — no word-splitting of a URL into extra arguments.
